newsitem.title: FRANCE: French assembly adopts private pension bill.
newsitem.headline: French assembly adopts private pension bill.

text.p: France's national assembly adopted on Wednesday, on second reading, a bill that will give about 14 million private sector French workers the option to set up private pensions savings accounts.
The bill was voted on by only 47 of the assembly's 577 parliamentarians, with 34 votes for and 13 against.
The low turnout was blamed on a long and raucous debate which lasted late into Tuesday night.
The bill now must be approved in its current form by the Senate, which is scheduled to take up the debate on January 30.
The government wants to give workers and companies the option to create another level of pensions.

It said the pension funds, which operate on a system of capitalisation whereby people save for their own pensions, will complement the distribution system under which pensioners are paid out of payroll charges on the workforce.
It hopes the pension funds will also boost the stock market and help channel resources into copanies' shares.

But French trade unions fear the introduction of pension funds will drain money from the distribution system and may be the first step in a run-down of the deficit-burdened welfare system, which covers health care, pensions and family benefits.
The government has taken pains to reassure unions that is not the case.
President Jacques Chirac, seeking to calm union fears, said on Wednesday he would personally guarantee that the new pension funds would not threaten France's traditional pension system.

"The distribution system is the foundation of our retirements. We are not considering questioning it and I am its guarantor," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as saying after a cabinet meeting.
He said the planned private pension funds "do not at all threaten the distribution system" of retirement pensions.

On Tuesday, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis sent out the same message. "There is no risk that the development of pension funds will be to the detriment of the distribution system which remains the fundamental element of our retirement system," he told a conference.

"On the contrary, by strengthening our companies, they will encourage the creation of wealth and jobs and, therefore, increase the resources of the basic system in the medium and long-term," Arthuis said.
The new funds will be set up under voluntary agreements between companies and their employees and will be given tax benefits.
The plans are part of an overall tax reform designed to funnel French savings into productive investment, thereby fuelling growth and helping to bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment.
Until the recent reduction in interest rates, most savings went largely to money market funds, dubbed "sleeping money" by the government.
